expansion:
A one‑month‑old infant who has photophobia, watering and a clear but markedly enlarged cornea fits the classic description of buphthalmos, the infantile manifestation of congenital glaucoma. The lecture lists the hallmark symptoms of congenital/developmental glaucoma as "Photophobia, watering, blepharospasm" and notes the presence of a "Large eye" (L12, slide 12). It also describes the ocular signs of this disorder, including an "enlarged corneal diameter" and a "broad limbus" (L12, slide 13). These features arise because elevated intra‑ocular pressure in the immature sclera causes globe enlargement, a process explicitly outlined in the pathogenesis slide (L12, slide 10). Therefore option D correctly identifies the diagnosis.

Congenital dacryocystitis (option A) presents with epiphora and discharge due to obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct, but it does not produce corneal enlargement or photophobia, and the tear passages are noted as normal in the stem, contradicting this diagnosis (not taken from the course material).

Interstitial keratitis (option B) is characterized by stromal infiltrates, vascularisation and corneal opacities, not a clear, enlarged cornea; photophobia may occur, but the cornea is not clear nor enlarged (not taken from the course material).

Keratoconus (option C) is a progressive ectasia seen in older children or adolescents, leading to a conical, thinned cornea rather than an enlarged clear cornea; it never presents in a one‑month‑old infant (not taken from the course material).
objective: Identify the ocular condition in an infant with photophobia, watering and an enlarged clear cornea.
